speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: HUNGARY
subsubtopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TRADE, EX- CHANGE OF DIPLOMATIC MISSIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representatives of the governments of Canada and the Hungarian People's Republic have held a number of meetings in Ottawa between May 20 and June 9 to discuss problems of common interest in the fields of trade, financial claims, consular matters and diplomatic relations.
In addition to an agreement on trade on which my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be making a statement, we have also agreed to an exchange of diplomatic missions with Hungary as soon as convenient to each party.
We have reached agreement with the Hungarian government to negotiate at an early date a settlement of outstanding financial claims between the two countries. I shall shortly be making an announcement of the type of claims which might be eligible for consideration under this agreement.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we have reached an understanding with the Hungarian government on a number of consular matters which will, among other things, clarify the position of Canadian citizens, including those of Hungarian origin, who may wish to travel in Hungary.
I propose now, Mr. Speaker, to table the letters I have exchanged today with the Hungarian vice minister for foreign affairs covering these various subjects.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: HUNGARY
subsubtopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TRADE, EX- CHANGE OF DIPLOMATIC MISSIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the three year trade agreement signed this morning between Canada and the Hungarian People's Republic is the first such agreement between the two countries in the post-war period.
The agreement is based on an exchange of most favoured nation treatment. At the same time Hungary has committed itself to purchase Canadian wheat and other goods to a total value of $24 million over the period
of the agreement. I would draw the attention of the house to the mixed nature of this purchase commitment, marking a departure from other recent agreements. Since Hungary itself is normally an exporter of wheat, that portion of its commitment involving wheat is to amount to 250,000 metric tons, a somewhat smaller quantity than has been involved in recent purchases by other countries. Hungary has the choice of taking one half of this amount in the form of feed barley. The remainder of the purchase commitment will be taken up by Hungary in the form of Canadian goods of its choice. These goods are not specified, but it is hoped that on the basis of past Hungarian interest, new and continuing markets will be opened up for a wide range of Canadian goods.
In addition, the agreements signed today provide that a Hungarian trade office may be opened in Canada and a Canadian trade office may be opened in Hungary for the purpose of market exploration and trade promotion. Both governments have expressed the wish that through these agreements trade between Canada and Hungary may be expanded on a mutually satisfactory basis.
The establishment of trade relations with Hungary represents yet another step in the development of closer trade links between Canada and the countries of eastern Europe. In recent years our long standing trade relations with Poland and Czechoslovakia have been further strengthened through our sales of wheat to these countries. Poland is currently discussing in the GATT the basis of its participation in the Kennedy round, and Canada has expressed support for this initiative. Our trade agreement with the Soviet union signed in 1956 has been twice renewed, and the first trade agreement between Canada and Bulgaria was concluded last year. I am sure that our new trade agreement with Hungary will make a further valuable contribution to the expansion of Canadian trade.
With the permission of the house I should like to table a copy of the trade agreement and other correspondence exchanged between the two governments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought I should announce briefly to the house and to the public that it is the intention of the government to seek the revision at an early date of the Canada-United Kingdom income tax agreement. An announcement that this agreement would be revised was first made by the then minister of finance in December, 1960, following his proposal that certain special rates of non-resident withholding tax on dividends be withdrawn and that a rate of 15 per cent thereafter be imposed on all dividends paid to non-residents. The intention to revise certain international income tax agreements was also stated in the budget speech of 1963.
1 have recently written to the chancellor of the exchequer in the United Kingdom suggesting that the discussions which were commenced in 1961 concerning the Canada-United Kingdom income tax agreement be reopened as soon as possible. If any hon. members or other persons or business firms wish to submit suggestions concerning the revision of this treaty, I would be glad to receive them during the next several weeks.

The house resumed, from Wednesday, June 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-100, to amend the Farm Credit Act-Mr. Hays-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Farming.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I was saying yesterday, war should be declared against the agricultural depression prevailing in Quebec ridings, an unrelenting war where technology, financial resources and all our talents would be used to find solutions acceptable to our farmers. At the same time we would wage war against hunger, want and collective poverty. As legislators, we should be more conscious of our responsibilities and we would perhaps be more worthy then of our title of representatives of the people.
Before I conclude, I should like to direct one question to the minister. Could he tell us whether he will consider the possibility of having the corporation reduce its interest rates, change the conditions concerning loan applications and see how it could contribute

financially to the establishment of markets for farm products? When can we expect a reply?
I am also asking the minister whether the government will soon make a decision as to the possibility of granting subsidies for grain shipping by truck right to the farm. Such a measure, requested by several farmers' associations, would be a great help, and I cannot see why the government could not comply with such a request.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few comments on this particular item, and I am going to relate my remarks rather exclusively to the particular clause itself although I may have to wander a little bit in order to make the point I think I should make. Subsection 2 raises some questions in my mind as to whether this amending bill is departing from the original purposes for which the legislation was conceived.
In order to refresh our memories as to what that purpose was I would like to refer to section 16 of the act which, as I understand it, has not been amended. If it has been amended I would be glad to have the minister tell me. Section 16 (b) reads:
Loans under this act shall be made only to farmers who are actually engaged In or are shortly to become engaged In the operation of the mortgaged farm and whose experience, ability and character are such as to warrant the belief that the farm to be mortgaged will be successfully operated;
These are wise, sensible and realistic provisions, and should be the kernel around which all this legislation is built; but looking at some of the amendments proposed in this bill I am wondering whether we are in fact departing from that particular principle. My reason is not only a general one in so far as the value of the legislation to the country as a whole is concerned, but I think I am entitled to relate this to the situation in my area and in the northern parts of Canada.
To emphasize this point I want to refer very briefly to a pamphlet issued by the Canadian council of resource ministers, volume 1, No. 3, for March, 1964. In that pamphlet there is a comment with regard to the particular area in which I am interested with respect to the application of the act and this particular amendment to the act. I am only going to give a digest of it, but I think it is quite important.
Homesteading, the historic method of settlement on the prairies, is undergoing a revival in the virgin lands of northern Alberta. A farm land boom has been under way since 1961. In

that first year, 1,371 applications were recorded. During the next year, to March 31, 1963, a total of 2,350 applications were received, and in the current year, to February 26, 2,350 applications have been filed.
In other words, in something less than three years over 6,000 applications for new land have been received from people proposing to go on the land and farm it. I think this area is probably one of the few left in Canada where we find a variation from the normal pattern of people leaving farms. The minister visited this area last winter and will bear me out in what I say. Here in the northern part of Alberta people are going on the land. But having in mind the nature of farming, the cost of breaking, brushing and clearing land and the cost of machinery and equipment, in order to farm the land effectively, produce efficiently and make a contribution to the economy of the country, certain financial assistance is required, and this legislation has been most effective in providing it.
I can say that in the quarter of a century before this act came into effect less than half a million dollars was lent under the old farm loan board in the entire northwestern part of Alberta, including all of Peace River constituency. I do not have the precise figure, but I believe that in the last four years loans have aggregated approximately $12 million. So we have the striking contrast of half a million dollars lent in 25 years and $12 million in four years. This indicates the intense interest that I, on behalf of the people of my constituency and in other northern areas, have in this matter, and why I question whether in what the minister is proposing we are not possibly departing from the main purpose of the legislation.
What is this purpose? If one looks at the annual reports of the Farm Credit Corporation over a number of years we find a very interesting contrast. In the fiscal year 1957-58 moneys used to purchase land were limited to 27.7 per cent of the total amount lent. For the fiscal year 1962-63 the amount for land purchases and improvements represented 66.8 per cent. In other words there has been a doubling.
This is the manner in which the utmost value will be obtained from this legislation, by the money being used to buy land, to make improvements and to purchase cattle. On the reverse side of the picture, in 1957-58 the amount of money used to pay off land and other debts was approximately 56.6 per cent. In the last fiscal year for which we have information, 1962-63, this was reduced to 20220-266

approximately 30 per cent. I think this is also a very necessary and wise change in the trend.
Having laid that foundation, let us look at this particular clause, and I am going to deal particularly with subclause 2, which reads as follows:
For the purposes of part II the corporation may deem the executor or the administrator of the estate of a deceased farmer to be a farmer within the meaning of paragraph (e) of subsection 1.
This raises two sincere questions in my mind which I think the minister might consider. First, what about the situation of an executor or administrator which is a trust company? As I understand the legislation, it is not intended to be applied to limited corporations save only those corporations which are defined as family corporations under the pertinent regulations. I have not the section at hand, but I am sure the minister can ascertain what it is from his officials. The legislation is applicable to farm corporations as defined in the regulations.
I pose this question to the minister. A trust company, which is a limited company, of course, either by act of parliament or under the pertinent companies act of the province or of the federal government, is certainly not a farming corporation as defined by the regulations. I am not opposed in a limited way to what is suggested here, but I wonder whether the minister in his consideration of this particular subsection would not find it necessary to spell out the matter in detail if it is proposed to extend this particular benefit to an executor or administrator which happens to be a limited company.
I am thinking of the responsibility which otherwise might be thrust upon the very hard working and efficient officials and employees of the Farm Credit Corporation who may have to decide questions of this kind, which I think should be decided here in parliament and not left to the discretion of the officials.
Second, I put this question to the minister. In doing so I have in mind the purpose of the act as set out in section 16 (b) where it is provided as follows:
Loans under this act shall be made only to farmers who are actually engaged in or are shortly to become engaged in the operation of the mortgaged farm and whose experience, ability and character are such as to warrant the belief that the farm to be mortgaged will be successfully operated.
I can visualize cases where the farmer has made his application and while the documents are in the process of being prepared he passes away. His administrator or executor would then be able to apply under this

Farm Credit Act
particular amendment. How would the officials deal with such a case, having in mind the fact that they must take into consideration the provisions of section 16 (b)? Take the situation where there is a widow with young children. How would it be possible for the officials to be able to say that the particular loan was being made to a farmer actually engaged in or shortly to become engaged in the operation of the mortgaged farm?
Certainly the particular circumstances will have to be considered. If the deceased farmer left an adult son or sons who are on the farm and who have made their intention to continue the farming operation plain to the corporation, then discretion could be exercised and there would be compliance with the principle of the act which is the kernel of the whole scheme. But if this is not done I can see situations arising where this particular subclause could be invoked and could be used only for the purpose of settling estates.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief. I simply want to commend the government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) for the fine legislation submitted to the house, to double the borrowing power of our farmers.
To my mind, Mr. Chairman, this legislation will be a stimulating one for our farmers, and more particularly those of the province of Quebec, who, I think, suffer from an "inferiority complex".
Too many farmers in the province of Quebec are afraid to increase their farming operations, and if today, there are complaints that so many farms do not pay their way, for instance in the riding of Lotbiniere, 1,100 farms have a gross income of less than $2,500 a year it may result from certain farm policies, but it is also due to the fact that too many farmers do not want to expand their operations, enlarge their acreage.
Consequently, the fact of granting them increased borrowing power will incite them to extend their acreage and to own larger farm units, thus increasing their productivity and, hence, their income.
I therefore congratulate the government for introducing such a measure and, if I may, I shall make a suggestion to the minister. Our farmers have vented certain grievances, which, I think, are quite justified, and I would more particularly draw the minister's attention to the following case. Several farmers in my riding who made loan applications to the Farm Credit Corporation, complain, and rightly so, that the evaluation process is very slow; too much time goes by before someone comes around to set a value on their farm and tell them whether they are entitled to a loan.
I therefore call the attention of the minister to this situation which affects our farmers, and I would ask him to have the procedure accelerated, so that the evaluation of those farms is done more quickly and that the farmers who apply for a loan get their answer sooner.

speechtext:
Perhaps I can claim to have more knowledge of farm loans than any other member of the house. Certainly I had more to do with the veterans farm loan board than any other member remaining in the house at the present time.
From 1943 until 1950 I was trying to rehabilitate the boys who came back from the war. At that time we had men in the field


who very often knew little or nothing about land values. We had difficulties in getting these boys installed on farms which were suitable for making a living. We had to intercede for them, otherwise they would have found it almost impossible to get the land. I have had a lot to do with the Farm Credit Corporation and with the farm loan board before that. I have great respect for the men who have been at the head of that organization, Mr. Rutherford, in the first place and then Mr. Owens. I know both of these gentlemen very well. They have been doing an excellent job. One cannot expect these men to be responsible for all the mistakes which are made. They have field men out in the field who make many of these decisions. They should be very particular men and do their jobs well.
You cannot always judge these matters strictly according to the value of the farm; you must take into consideration the man who is seeking the loan. Sometimes you get a young man who wants to start farming but he does not have any considerable amount of money. Yet his reputation is good and if given a chance it is not long before he makes a name for himself. The point is this; It is getting harder and harder to start boys on a farm if they do not have money. When I started farming I started with practically nothing and worked my way up in a few years so that I was able to get a little credit. But a boy cannot even start farming nowadays unless he has, say, $10,000. A boy who is inclined to favour agriculture finds it difficult to get enough money to start, and his only hope lies in the farm loan board. You cannot get private mortgages any more because the money lenders will not lend money to farmers.
I have read over this bill and I am not entirely against the amendments being sought. However I have not studied them sufficiently well to pass an opinion on them. I am inclined to be dubious about parts of the bill and I think perhaps I will wait until the other clauses come up for consideration before I pass judgment on them. I wanted to say something because of the fact that I have had so much to do with farm loans during the years trying to get these boys started on farms. Many of the older men who have boys coming along find it difficult to carry on without the help of the boys, and the boys find that unless father has a little money to give them they cannot get started on their own.

The minister said he was anxious about boys 16, 17 and 18 years of age. Mind you, there is an awful lot of difference in boys. You get a boy sometimes who is almost a man by the time he is 16 and you get another who does not develop until he is 20, 21 or 22. Take a boy who is level headed and interested in farming. At 16 he is as good a man as he will ever be and can do as much work. I think the minister is justified in looking after loans of this sort.
I am not so sure about how the interest rates are to be arrived at. I think it should be set down in clear words; there should be no guesswork. I agree that the interest rate is not to be increased above 5 per cent in respect of loans up to $20,000 and, in another case, up to $27,500. But 1 am not sure what the intention is with regard to loans outside that category. I will try to find out before the bill goes through.
Let us bear in mind that for as long as I can remember-and that is a long time- farmers have always been short of money. Some farmers of course have been lent money. But the man who has to earn his income on a farm is generally short of money and the only way in which he can get along is by means of loans from the government. I do not want to see interest rates jacked up until the loan is impossible to repay. Some people say: What about industry? That is another matter. Industry makes more money than farming does, and a farmer cannot be expected to pay the kind of rates expected from industry. I hope that when the other clauses come before the committee I will be able to understand them a little better.

Mr. Chairman, rising to take part in the debate on clause 1 of Bill No. C-100 I would first like to congratulate the farm credit officials for the wonderful job they have done in administering this act and making it applicable to many of the farm areas throughout Canada. Certainly, no matter how good the act is, amendments are required from time to time to keep up with and ahead of the expanding economy and the expanding circumstances of farming and agriculture. I think, though, that in some respects the amendments before us today will have a tendency to narrow the application of the Farm Credit Act, rather than widen it.
I am somewhat concerned to see in the 1962-63 annual report, the last one that is available, that on page 5 it states that during the fiscal year some 21,000 farmers consulted
Farm Credit Act
the corporation, and it goes on to state that only 9,875 received loans; 46 per cent completed formal loan applications. I am concerned about the other 11,000 people who did not get loans and whether the act was suitable for the type of loan about which they consulted the corporation. I think that, rather than increasing the amount available we should make the money that is now available applicable to more farmers in more areas of Canada.
It pleases me a great deal to see at the top of page 5 that the Farm Credit Corporation in its fourth annual report had this to say with regard to the amendments brought in in 1962. It is said that the amendment of the Farm Credit Act in November, 1962, "will considerably enlarge the scope of the corporation's future lending activity". This is the type of legislation we brought in at that time; we allowed farmers to borrow money on the income they earned outside of their direct income from the farm. This in some way must have brought in some of the 11,000 persons who approached the corporation the year before last-and in fact approach them every year-and did not get a loan because their cases were perhaps not suitable for receiving a loan from the corporation.
While I have this annual report in my hands I think it should be pointed out, as it probably has been a number of times already, that of the some 7,000 loans approved, the average loan was a little better than $12,000. As the minister pointed out in his speech opening this debate, only some 11 per cent of those who applied for a loan asked for the maximum amount available. This makes me wonder whether increasing these loans to $40,000 and $55,000 is actually meeting the requirements of the many people who applied for loans and did not receive them. I think perhaps the Farm Credit Corporation's greatest benefit to farmers is its attitude toward establishing young farmers, farmers on uneconomic units and small farmers; to get them on their feet and up to the standard of an economic unit. There has been a great deal of talk regarding what is an economic unit. I imagine the minister has his own views in this respect I am led to believe that in the minister's view an economic unit would be a very large one indeed, as he is sponsoring maximum loans of $40,000 and $55,000. It is not that I have anything against loans of this size because I well realize that many farms cost a great deal to maintain and operate. However, I also realize that in order for a farmer to borrow $40,000 or $55,000 from the

Farm Credit Act
Farm Credit Corporation he must himself have in the neighbourhood of from $10,000 to $20,000 to apply to the farm.
This brings me to the point, Mr. Chairman, as to how many small farmers can take advantage of a $40,000 loan when they must have 25 per cent of that amount in cash or negotiable securities in order for their application to be approved by the Farm Credit Corporation. Certainly not many farmers in my area have $10,000 in negotiable securities which they could put forward on an application for a loan of $40,000 from the corporation.
I am greatly concerned that making this large amount of money available will be of direct benefit to the large farmers and of no real benefit, or very small benefit, to the small farmers. Some 54 per cent of the people who consulted the Farm Credit Corporation nearly every year find that the corporation does not meet their needs with regard to loans. Perhaps the same 54 per cent reappear the next year and are able to find their needs fulfilled; I have no doubt that this is the case on many occasions. But I am concerned about the 54 per cent who are turned away or who leave on their own account. I do not think a $40,000, or a $55,000 loan under part III, will in any way help these 54 per cent who are turned away every year and find that the Farm Credit Corporation is not meeting their needs.
One must look at farm income, at the products produced in the various areas of Canada, to see whether the farmers in these areas would be able to pay back a loan of this large amount. When you consider the statistics of the last census in 1961 you realize that some 480,000 farmers in Canada had an average realized net income, even in the more prosperous provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the prairies, perhaps, of less than $3,000 a year. This leads me to believe, once again, that the average farmer cannot make use of a $55,000 loan which will be the maximum obtainable when this measure is passed. We realize that in some areas of Canada agriculture lags behind other areas. Some parts of Quebec and the mar-itimes have not really taken full advantage of the Farm Credit Corporation. In 1962-63 only some 60 loans were made in the province of Nova Scotia; this compares with some 2,000 in Saskatchewan, I think. When one looks at the income figures for these provinces-I think the realized net income figure for the average farm in the province of Quebec was something like $1,200, and the maritimes was
[Mr. Horner (Acadia) .1
not too much higher-he understands why farmers in those areas cannot pay back a huge loan of $40,000 or $55,000. This convinces me that these amendments will be directly aimed at benefiting the large farmer.
When the Farm Credit Corporation was set up in 1959 I thought its main purpose was to help only those farmers who needed money, those farmers who were farming on what could be termed relatively uneconomic units. I thought this was a wonderful principle which would help raise the standard of living on farms all across Canada, and in it I saw hope for many farmers and particularly those who most needed a loan.
I have the feeling, in view of these amendments to the act, that the principle of the Farm Credit Corporation will slowly change and go back to the old idea that those who have the most will get the most by way of loans. This is a fear which I feel I should express at this time. Up to this point I think the corporation has done a wonderful job to help farmers who really need a loan, but I fear that increasing the amount of the loan will perhaps destroy the initial principle on which the Farm Credit Corporation was founded.
I also think that under clause 3 a greater erosion of this principle is feasible. The clause suggests that a father, uncle or brother can borrow money on behalf of a son, son-in-law, daughter, daughter-in-law, nephew, niece and so on. This may sound good, but it may well allow-and I should like to know whether or not it will allow- a farmer operating what is now classified as a commercialized enterprise and who is not entitled to a loan from the corporation, to borrow money for his son who, by reason of age, is not yet able to carry on the farm. Perhaps the son is 12, 14 or even 16 and still at school; and we all hope that he will stay at school for as long as he can. But this clause may well allow a farmer who was not otherwise entitled to a loan to borrow money on his own credentials for his son, son-in-law and so on, and in fact create even a larger corporation around him and his family. Perhaps I see greater dangers in the clause than are evident to the minister.
The hon. member for Peace River suggested that the settlement of an estate could also lead to a corporate type of operation in a case where the initial borrower dies, leaving a wife and several children to carry on the repayment of the loan while the farm operation is managed in trust, perhaps by a trust company for all we know. This would tend to

direct money advanced by the Farm Credit Corporation into the more commercialized operation, the sort of operation which really would not qualify under the initial principle of the Farm Credit Corporation, which was to help those who needed help most.
I noticed that at the beginning of the minister's remarks in introducing the debate he stated that the principle of the Farm Credit Corporation was to make loans for the buying of livestock and equipment, as well as to improve farm buildings and houses. If one looks at the money which has been paid out by the Farm Credit Corporation, some 80 per cent of it has been directed toward paying land debts and buying more land, whereas only some 3 per cent was applied to the purchase of livestock.
The minister went on to point out that another principle of the Farm Credit Corporation was to assist the small farmer to expand his enterprise to an economical size. I wonder whether the minister could give us some idea as to what he feels is an economical size, not in acreage but as far as capitalization is concerned. Perhaps the corporation have some figures they use as a rough guide which in turn will guide the committee this afternoon in its discussion of this bill.
I am also concerned at the rate of interest payable on loans over $20,000 and $27,500 under part III. In some respects perhaps it is an established principle that, if one has a sound credit rating, the more money one borrows from the bank the lower the interest rate. But here it is the opposite: the more money one borrows the higher the interest rate. A high interest rate on a large loan makes it all the more difficult to meet the repayments. One hon. member mentioned that a loan of $55,000 taken over 35 years would mean that a borrower had paid back $125,000 at the end of the term. This gives the committee some idea as to what this interest rate means; it means a lot of money to the person who is repaying the loan.
I, like the former speaker, should like to see the interest rates spelled out in the bill so that the farmers would know exactly what this means to them. A farmer taking a $25,000 loan under part II of the act would perhaps be better advised to borrow the money under part III of the act unless the interest rate made a great difference. He would have to get advice from the corporation, but it might save him the difference in interest between the rate on $20,000 and that on $27,500. That may be an avenue which could be explored.
Farm Credit Act
The minister stated that in some respects these amendments are reinforcing the position of family farms. I have grave doubts whether this would be accomplished. The average family farm, judging from the 480,000 farmers in Canada, involves a capitalization around $30,000; and nearly half our farmers have an acreage of 250 acres or less. As a result of the amendments I am afraid that the capital will be slowly drawn off, and perhaps not immediately but in the ensuing years there will be a tendency for the corporation to place large sums of money in good secure hands, but it will not bring about the improvement in over-all farm standards which we should like to see.
I realize that the Farm Credit Corporation is sometimes rather a stickler, with regard to making loans, in ensuring that a farmer borrows enough money to establish himself on what the corporation calls an economical unit. I have had a number of farmers come to me and tell me they want to borrow only $3,000 or $4,000, but that the corporation has said that that was no good, that they should find a farm value at $20,000 and that they would receive a loan of $20,000. That is why these amendments concern me today. There are a number of farmers-I am sure this is the case in many areas of Canada-who, having farmed a half section of land for the last ten years, suddenly find available a quarter section of land adjacent to their own farm.
They want to buy this and it can be bought for $5,000 or $6,000. However, the corporation says, "No; this still does not give you an economic unit in our way of thinking and we would not lend you $5,000 or $6,000, but if you find a bigger farm, a well established farm, we will lend you $20,000." This may sound good in principle but many cases have been pointed out to me where a farmer, who has existed for ten years on a half section of land, sees a piece of land adjacent to him that he wants, but the corporation will not lend him the money to buy it. As the years go by maybe another quarter section would become available and eventually he would be able to establish himself on a full economic unit.
I also believe the corporation should continue to make and process loans throughout the winter. It has been its policy not to make appraisals after the first snow flies, but at times it is pretty difficult to shut down and wait until spring. You have other agencies and departments of government saying, "Do it now; why wait till spring?" But the

Farm Credit Act
corporation takes the attitude that once the first snow flies it must shut down on appraisals and wait until spring.
Perhaps the Farm Credit Corporation might not be as brave in its winter appraisals as in its summer ones, but it could process applications and perhaps not pay loans on as large a scale as in the summer months. In this connection I am thinking of a particular case of a farmer who had rented a place for five or six years. He knew it as well as he knew his own place. The owner died and, in order for the estate to be settled, the farm had to be sold, and this man could not wait until spring to obtain the money to buy the farm. If the corporation had been taking applications and appraising land during the winter months he could have enlarged his farm. I am sure this situation exists in many parts of Canada.
In Alberta last winter many southern parts had no snow, but the corporation claimed the ground was frozen and it could not make an appraisal. There is no real difficulty in taking a chunk of frozen ground into a house, thawing it out, and conducting a soil test on it. For that reason I say this is one particular regulation that could be removed.
Under the terms of this bill we are asked to place our judgment in the hands of the corporation with regard to estate administrators, and with regard to people borrowing money on behalf of their sons or sons-in-law. Up to the present time the corporation has done a real good job in administering the act. I have full confidence in it, and I believe it could process many applications throughout the winter months in many parts of Canada. This would be an additional benefit to small farmers who need money during the winter when pieces of land come up for sale.
In closing I say that if the minister is trying to assist the small farmer, to strengthen and reinforce the family farm, he should give further consideration to the amendments he proposes. To me it appears that increasing the amounts of loans to $40,000 and $50,000 is a millionaire's approach to the solution of agricultural problems. It may be of real benefit to some farmers, to a small percentage of the applicants, but I greatly fear that many of the 55 per cent of the applicants who are turned down, or who go away from the corporation of their own accord each year, will not benefit very much from this proposal.
The minister has said further amendments will be necessary. I hope he gives greater

consideration to some amendments which would be more beneficial to the small farmers across Canada.

The whole problem with farming is that those farmers who are operating at a subsistence level must have their operations converted into an economic unit, and certainly it will take a great deal more credit if he is going to be able to repay.

Mr. Chairman, the more I listen to the minister the more I am convinced that he has completely missed the purpose of this legislation when it was first introduced in the House of Commons. I do not take exception to legislation which will provide an increase in the amount of loans where a larger loan can be made use of, unless we are to have the increase without also broadening the scope of the act to take care of the 11,000 farmers per year who have
Farm Credit Act
been unable to take advantage of the act as it is now constituted.
A few minutes ago something was said by the hon. member for Lotbiniere about the problems in his area. I listened to the minister's remarks yesterday and today and it seems to me that the whole situation has escaped him, so far as the need of people faced with a particular problem is concerned. Before we proceed to broaden the act to make loans in excess of $27,500 available and double the amount available for individual farm units, I believe that something should be done for the vast number of farm people to be found in every part of the country who up to now have been unable to benefit from the legislation.
In saying that, I am not discrediting the legislation that has been brought forward or the good work that has been done by the officials who have tried to put the legislation into effect for the benefit of agriculture. All of us know that the legislation introduced in 1959, and amended later, requires further amendment from time to time to meet situations as they arise. Surely we have learned something from the experience of the last few years. In looking at the record of loans the thing that impresses me most is that the losses have been so small. That being so, it would seem to me that because of the regulations that have been in effect we surely must have been bypassing a great number of farmers who deserve loans.
I should like the minister to give more than passing consideration to this problem. I am disturbed by the legislation as presented, particularly clause 3 which enables the borrower to acquire farmland for his son or daughter, and so on. There is nothing wrong with that in itself, but it indicates the trend of thinking of the government. We must realize that land is getting scarcer in Canada today and that the purpose of establishing the Farm Credit Corporation was to bring as many people as possible into active agricultural production. The amendments before us today have the reverse effect. Unless the minister is prepared to introduce more lenient regulations so as to make loans available to those who have been unable to qualify in the past, I believe that the amendments before us today will have a very serious effect on the agricultural situation in Canada. They can only have one result, that there will be fewer farmers. Perhaps some people think this is inevitable, and maybe it is; but surely we should try to see that the development of these resources is

left in the hands of as many families as possible and not try to funnel these resources into the hands of a smaller number of families.
I think it is a well known fact that the farmer who is well established is better able to establish his sons, daughters and other relatives in agriculture or, for that matter, in any other business. Those who need help are those who are not as well established. Perhaps this whole point is not making a dent on the minister at all but I hope he will take it under consideration and give it the attention it deserves.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few comments on the bill to amend the Farm Credit Act. My only purpose in rising is because of certain statements made by the hon. member for Essex South yesterday. As found on page 4162 of Hansard, he said:
All that was said yesterday by the members of the opposition added up to one thing, that for the last six years they have recognized that the Farm Credit Corporation was not meeting the needs of agriculture.
He made that statement just after talking about a windstorm, and I think that windstorm must have affected his words. The Farm Credit Corporation deserves a tremendous amount of credit. I think members have only to recall the old Canadian farm loan board, which in its day did a good job within the limitations placed upon it. But when the Farm Credit Corporation took over in 1959 it adopted a new approach to the credit and other needs of farmers all over Canada. I do not want to make a political speech but I would remind members opposite who have been criticizing the Farm Credit Corporation that it was set up by a Conservative administration.
The basic difference was that, instead of just looking at loans on the basis of proper security, as the farm loan board did, the Farm Credit Corporation looked at the needs of the farmers from the point of view of what constituted an economic unit. The minister has made much of the fact that the farm must be an economic unit in order to repay the loan. I think that has been the basis of all loans made by the corporation to date.
As far as my area is concerned, we do not have too much mixed farming. There is a certain amount of lumbering and some raising of cattle but mainly we have orchards. The benefits which have accrued to these orchardists in British Columbia through the Farm Credit Corporation are immense. In many cases the whole picture has been
[Mr. Nasserden.l
changed, and this has continued year after year.
One has only to examine the loans made to see what an excellent job the Farm Credit Corporation has done. I was extremely pleased to hear the hon. member for Huron speak this afternoon. Because of his great knowledge of farming I was particularly pleased with the pat on the back he gave the Farm Credit Corporation. He comes from eastern Canada and I felt that his words supported what I intended to say this afternoon. There have been complaints with regard to the time it takes to have appraisals made. I have checked into a great many complaints over the last number of years and I would say that if all appraisals were to be made quickly, in the rush of the season, the corporation would require a staff far greater in numbers than what they now have and they would have to be on the job 24 hours a day. I do not blame the Farm Credit Corporation at all for this. We have a longer period during the year in which appraisals can be made. However, you cannot just go out and pick up people off the street and say, "You are an appraiser; go out and look at farms." You have to have men with proper training and an understanding of farm problems.
I must say that in my area of British Columbia the appraisers are good. I can say they are men of understanding, Mr. Chairman, because they are faced with a great many problems when men cannot understand why their application for loans have been turned down. Certainly, we have a backlog of applicants for loans, but you cannot have an immediate appraisal. I would say offhand that there seems to be some concern about the number of applicants who were turned down last year. However if I am any judge of the applicants, the type of men who are processing and of the type of men who form the administration of the Farm Credit Corporation, I would say that the vast majority of the applicants are requesting loans on non-economic units.
I thought the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Rosthern made excellent points. I should like to refer the minister to the amendments made in 1962. These were good amendments; they were broadening amendments. They gave applicants a better opportunity to qualify for loans, because income from other sources was considered to be income available for the repayment of the loans. I do not believe the doubling of the amount of credit available is the answer to this problem. I believe this is a good measure,

but I do not believe it will apply too much to my area. I can see that for the larger units on the prairies these provisions would be excellent.
The hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Rosthern both emphasized the fact that there should be a stronger attempt to keep the family on the farm. This might not be economic if credit were required to achieve this objective. 1 think the minister might look over the regulations under which this administration operates. Actually, I believe the administration is not hidebound. I believe they have a flexible way of looking at the requirements for credit of the individual orchardist or farmer. I feel that when a man makes application, if he has anything remotely resembling an economic unit he will get extraordinary consideration. It is true that in my area probably as much as anywhere, because of the nature of fruit farming and because of the nature of the economic unit needed, people asking for loans have been told that these loans will not do them any good. That what is needed is a larger loan so they can be put on an economic basis.
At the moment, as has been pointed out, there has been little if any loss to the Farm Credit Corporation because repayments have been made on a regular basis. May I say, in closing, that we have had a great many congratulatory messages to the minister from Liberal members? I do not want to detract in any way from those words but I should like to add that the work which was put in earlier made the Farm Credit Corporation an extraordinarily good means of extending credit to farmers all across Canada. Finally, I should like to say to the hon. member for Essex South that he should spend a little time talking to some of his colleagues, or some of us over here, in order to find out exactly what the Farm Credit Corporation is and just what it has done since its inception.

subtopic: MODELS FOR CANADIAN FLAG

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, June 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Smallwood:
That an order of the house do issue for the production of all flag designs or models which have been received by the Prime Minister, members of the cabinet or the government, as models for a Canadian flag.
Motions for Papers

subtopic: MODELS FOR CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
By the terms of the motion which the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood) has put before the house I take it he is hoping to have the property or ownership in every such flag design or flag model transferred to parliament. This may not have been the hon. member's intention, but I submit it will be the effect of ordering the production and tabling of more than 3,000 flag designs which, we are told, have been sent to and examined by the government, more particularly by the department of the Secretary of State.
In this situation I think the hon. member should consider whether such action does not in itself amount to an infringement or expropriation of copyright and be actionable in the courts in each case by writ of summons or petition of right. Further, even if no action were brought in respect of an individual design there likely could be no redelivery to the sender or author upon request unless this house, which is sovereign, ordered such redelivery. All hon. members might just imagine for one moment the effect of having individual writs of summons issued or individual requests made to obtain these numerous flag designs and models. Failing an order by the house for redelivery in a particular case, the government could again be faced with a writ of summons or a petition of right in many cases. I do not argue that a writ or petition would be issued in respect of each flag design or model, but there could be a sufficient number to make this house regret the day when the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose bestowed himself on his electors and inflicted this motion upon the house.
The likelihood is enhanced by the publicity which has already been given to this motion. I am sure that many authors of flag designs and flag models which have been submitted are now acutely conscious of their proprietary interest in their creative work, both by virtue of common law and by virtue of a federal statute, the Copyright Act. Furthermore, many authors who have sent in their submissions specifically requested that their designs be returned to them. Thus, to impound their creations by passing this motion would, I submit, amount to an inexcusable breach of faith as well as a breach of this federal parliament's own law.
I have grave doubts-and I am sure they are shared by most hon. members-whether flag designs and flag models come under the definition of "papers". I would think that the rule might be applied to the letters and the briefs or instructions which accompanied
[The Chairman.)
these submissions, but not to the actual artistic works themselves. Certainly with respect to some designs and models at least, they are not papers at all-they are articles. We have heard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) describe one as being executed on a piece of plywood; I think it was six feet by three feet, or eight feet by four feet. This is certainly not a piece of paper.
All hon. members are aware-or they ought to be-that the guiding principle is that when papers are sought to be produced they should be of a public or official character, not of a private or confidential nature. In this case, the government did not invite, request or advertise for the submission of the thousands of models which have been sent in, as distinct from the case in 1946 when those who were asked to submit flag designs and models were told that they would be further submitted to a committee. In this case the government did not stipulate any use to which these designs or models might be put. They were sent in, for the most part voluntarily by public-spirited citizens who had a burning desire to see a distinctive national flag for this country. They were sent in also by professional designers and artists, all of them hoping, no doubt, that their work might be accepted either in whole or in part by the government when reaching its decision.
I believe, therefore, that implicit in the submission of each designer was the understanding that only after his work had been chosen, either in whole or in part, would there be any publication, reproduction, transfer or use of his design or model. Thus if it were thought desirable to produce and table these flag designs and flag models-and I do not agree with this assumption-I say that the only reasonable and proper thing to do would be to contact each of the authors and obtain a written assignment of ownership and copyright in each case. This would of course involve a delay of unforeseeable length, particularly because some of the authors would, no doubt, be extremely difficult to locate. In some cases, executors of estates would be required to sign. It is indeed unlikely that all the designs and models could ever be tabled with permission.
This motion has been a waste of the time of this house and it is no tribute to the mover's sense of responsibility or to that of his party. If, by some inconceivable circumstance, it were allowed to pass either in whole or in part, it would amount to a costly exercise in sheer futility. A flag design has already

been chosen by the government in pursuance of its commitment and responsibility. The situation as I see it is that the hon. member would like to hold his own beauty contest and select his own beauty queen, after the beauty queen has been chosen by the proper judges.
At this stage the motion would tend towards chaos rather than order in the field of choosing an official national flag for Canada. I am sure the house will see it simply as a clumsy attempt to postpone further the selection of a Canadian flag which should have been selected many years ago. The position of the mover with respect to this motion is currently far worse than it was last Thursday, because the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Stewart) in his usual inoffensive manner then offered to let the hon. member personally see and analyse all the designs and models in the hands of the department. The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose has not to date availed himself of this golden opportunity to exercise his flag picking fingers. Some people having this same opportunity might be tempted to design and obtain a copyright on the new game of "flagpik" and sell it to the Eskimos.
Mr. Speaker, without admitting that a flag design or flag model is a paper within the rules, I would probably not be so disturbed about this motion if it sought the production of flag designs or flag models within the public or international domains. I am thinking of such things as a black flag, either with or without the skull and crossbones, which in days gone by was the symbol of the pirate, or the plain yellow flag which was and still is the sign of infectious illness aboard ship-

AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EMPLOYEES IN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-45, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act (agricultural employees' coverage).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I had not expected that my bill would come up today. However, as it has been on the order paper for many sessions and parliaments I am prepared to suggest to the house that serious consideration be given to bringing agricultural employees under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Agricultural employees are the only employees not covered by unemployment insurance. This creates hardship on farmers who want to hire employees in the spring or fall, but because these employees are not covered by insurance the excuse is made that when their seasonal employment on the farm is over they will find themselves in a position where they are unable to keep their families, because during the time they were employed their incomes were too low. Consequently these people are not available, and they will not be available unless agricultural employees receive the same coverage under the Unemployment Insurance Act as do other employees.
The excuse has been made many times both by the minister and other government officials that no action can be taken until the Gill report is received, so that they can study the recommendations made. I have not got a copy of the report before me at the present time, but I might point out that the report recommends that all employees be covered by unemployment insurance, provided there are the proper administrative procedures or processes available. I cannot see why the administration of unemployment insurance for farm labourers should be so difficult or so different compared with employees in other industries.
For many years we in the west, where agriculture is perhaps on a somewhat larger scale than other places, have run into diffi-


culty at seeding or at harvest time when the rush is on, of being unable to get help. Many times farmers contact the unemployment offices in the cities to no avail. I should like the government to give serious consideration to the recommendation of the Gill commission to which I have referred, because the commission stress the point that agricultural employees and all other employees should be covered by unemployment insurance where the necessary administrative procedures are available. Therefore I ask the minister, or in his absence the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Byrne), to give serious consideration to this problem.
I well remember that in another parliament when I presented this bill many members of the party which now forms the government wholeheartedly supported its purposes. Now that the Liberal party is in power, I should like the members of parliament who so vigorously supported my bill previously to stand up and speak in its support as they did before. This bill raises a serious problem. It is most important that farm labourers be covered by unemployment insurance.
The agricultural industry in the west is becoming more mechanized, as a result of which it is difficult to get employees who know how to operate these big combines, tractors and other machines. Many farmers have incurred great losses on account of being unable to get help. As time goes on I think the need for agricultural employees able to work on these big farms will become smaller.
In conclusion, I should like to direct the attention of the parliamentary secretary, in the absence of the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), to the Gill report and I invite him to tell the house that my bill, Bill No. C-45, will be sent to the committee for discussion, instead of talking the bill out, as I expect will be the case. At the same time I would urge the government to give serious consideration to this matter and bring farm labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EMPLOYEES IN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member in moving second reading of this bill. We are all sympathetic to any objectives which try to develop the broadest possible coverage to employees under the Unemployment Insurance Act, and which try to see to it that every class of employee in Canada in gainful employment gets equal protection and rights

under our social security legislation, of which the Unemployment Insurance Act is an important part.
As a member of the house sitting on this side I have some reservations in my mind about the piecemeal attack on the problem of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act. The hon. member who proposes this legislation made reference to the report of the Gill committee in which was a general recommendation that the principle of extending insurance coverage should be given sympathetic consideration. The government is looking very carefully and systematically at the recommendations in the Gill report, and we would be more than irresponsible were we not to do so. But it is the intention of the government at the earliest possible date to place specific measures before this house involving a fairly substantial series of amendments to the act and changes in the operation of the fund.
We all know what happened to the unemployment insurance fund. We recall rather painfully that in 1957-58 there was close to $1 billion in that fund. We also recall very painfully that in 1963 the fund had to borrow money from the government of Canada to sustain its operations, and at one particular juncture in 1964 we had a rather embarrassing experience concerning the approval of the necessary authorities to make payments under this act.
There is no question, when looking at the extension of coverage of unemployment insurance, that we have to look at the record of the industry which is being covered. We know the problems of agriculture, that agriculture represents declining employment, that at present it means increasing size of farm units. Increased mechanization is becoming more and more a part of agriculture, and agriculture requires more and more capital. It is for these reasons that we have been debating authority, under another piece of legislation, to provide additional capital loans to farmers in order to help them increase their efficiency.
We know there are times of the year, as was pointed out by the hon. member proposing this bill, when there is a shortage of farm help. We are of course well aware of all this; but it does not necessarily follow that we can take the simplest and easiest type of resolution, which simply says we will give these benefits to this category of employees. We cannot do that, in view of the history of the unemployment fund.
Unemployment Insurance Act
If we believe in the principle of unemployment insurance-and I am very sure there are very few hon. members in the house who do not-then it follows that when we propose amendments to the legislation we have to look in an over-all way at the fiscal implication of what we are doing. The bill before us does not do that.
It has one curious clause which I personally found difficult to understand, and though I am sure the hon. member has taken professional advice on the matter, I have some doubts in my own thoughts as to whether this would stand up in the courts. The problem relates to private members' limitations in regard to the initiation of money bills. This clause proposes to restrict the payments that could be made to the amounts contributed by private individuals, to make sure that the contribution from the government of Canada is not paid out. The hon. member is making gestures. Does he disagree?

speechtext:
Shortly before five o'clock the Minister of Agriculture suggested that some $230 million in loans-I believe that was the figure he used-have been taken out by farmers from sources other than the Farm Credit Corporation. I do not know whether it was his intention to give the impression that with the passage of this bill the situation would be corrected or not, but if this was his intention I wish to make a few remarks at this moment to suggest something to the contrary.
I am suggesting that the reason $230 million was taken out in loans from sources other than the Farm Credit Corporation or other sources, such as those available under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, is that the provisions of the existing act do not permit farmers to obtain loans. The minister is aware that some 55 per cent of those who have gone to credit advisers for loans have not been able to obtain them. It is for this reason that they are obliged to resort to other sources. Many farmers with whom I am personally acquainted have had their applications for loans turned down by the Farm Credit Corporation for one reason or another, in most cases because in the opinion of the credit adviser the unit which is proposed to 
set up would not be an economic one. I know that in many cases farmers have had opportunities to acquire land adjacent to their own. While it is true that this particular purchase might not result in an economic unit in the eyes of the Farm Credit Corporation adviser, the farmer himself might have seen a possibility that in a few years someone else might have some suitable land to sell, and that the loan would place him in a better position to set up an economic unit later on. But because he is refused a loan by the Farm Credit Corporation, and because he feels his opportunity slipping away, he turns to other sources for finance. Many farmers in this situation turn to sources such as the credit unions. I understand that in most cases the credit unions charge a higher interest rate than that charged by the Farm Credit Corporation. But these farmers feel that unless they go ahead and borrow the money everything they had planned and hoped for will be lost; their chances will have slipped by, and henceforth they will be going backwards instead of forwards.
A farmer who has not been able to get a loan under this legislation certainly will not be able to do so as a result of the amendment proposed now. Nothing has been done to meet such a situation as I have described, and I suggest that next year we shall be able to look up the record and find that the situation is unchanged, that these people have had to go to other sources, and that because of the attitude taken by the farm credit board there has been a refusal to make loans where the proposition does not lead to the establishment of an economic unit.
I suggest that what has happened with regard to the bill before us is this: The minister found that in a few days the corporation would be short of funds. Thus, he had to come to parliament and ask for more funds. This is a necessary step, and I agree with it. At the same time, the minister felt he should, perhaps, throw in a few amendments for the sake of appearances. This I believe is exactly what he has done. In the first clause we find what in future years will amount to a lawyers' bonanza. I am sure the minister is trying to get across to the country that he is doing something for the farmers, but we shall find that the situation as it affects the 55 per cent who have been refused loans by the corporation has not been changed.
If the minister had made proposals for the setting up of an appeal board, for example,

it would have been a move in the right direction. An applicant whose request for a loan had been refused by a credit officer could then turn to a group of people and put forward his case with a view to having the decision reversed. If the minister does not want to set up an appeal board, I will make another suggestion. He could arrange for applications to be heard by a group of, say, half a dozen people, as is done by the credit unions in every community. They have groups of interested people and they perform this service for nothing, in a sense. They would, possibly, be familiar with the operation which the applicant had conducted and would be in a better position to know whether or not he was a good risk. If it were felt that the man could be regarded as a fair risk, the decision made by the credit officer could be reversed. This would constitute one method by which farmers whose applications for loans have been turned down in the past might qualify. I suggest this is the area in which there is most irritation.
I might just as well put on record a few of the other objections I have to this bill; it will save my having to get up later. I understand that the loans which may be made above $20,000 to $27,000 under the terms of the bill may amount to something in the order of 7 per cent, according to the figures I have been able to get from the minister's department. These figures would indicate that a loan of $55,000 over a period of 30 years under the new provisions would cost over $12,000 in interest, and so on. The former Conservative administration set the rate at 5 per cent. If the rate is going to be in the neighbourhood of 7 per cent, it will cost a farmer over $12,000 more for a loan of the same size as one he might have obtained under the provisions of the act as administered by the former government. This is a great deal of money when one considers that for a $55,000 loan he will repay almost $125,000 in 30 years.
I have another question for clarification, Mr. Chairman. When a farmer obtains a loan of over $27,500 under part II of the act I wonder what rate of interest the corporation will apply in collecting the money. If the farmer has finished paying off $27,500 at a rate over and above 5 per cent, will he be paying a lower rate of interest every year or will the calculation be made in such a way that each year the payments will be at the same rate? One other objection I have to the increase in the interest rate is that it will be a deterrent to the borrowing of
Farm Credit Act
money. Farmers will hesitate if the interest rate is higher than it was the previous year; they will say, "Perhaps it will be lower next year, so I will not get a loan this year". This in itself will have a deterring effect. I think the minister wants to leave the impression that he is doing something for the farmers, but certainly this provision, whereby the farmer will not know what the rate is going to be and will perhaps assume it will be lower next year, will mean he will not rush in to get a loan and in many cases this could mean he would be giving up an opportunity that might never again occur in his lifetime.
I wonder whether the minister would consider giving at least an idea as to whether the interest rate will be set for one year and the next year it might be changed, or whether interest rates will be changed monthly or every half year. These are just a few of the objections I have in this connection, Mr. Chairman, and any other questions I have I will raise at the appropriate time.

Mr. Chairman, in this era of automation, technology and machines, the minister who is actively involved with the ARDA program at the present time will eventually be able to deal with a larger movement of farmers who have become employees and who will become then regular unemployed or people living in the most abject misery. Why? Because we are now trying harder to dispossess

them, allegedly because they cannot live on the income from their farm. That reminds me of the Quebec farmer who took the plane for the first time and who, while flying at 15,000 feet-

I would say the same thing about the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), who is responsible for ARDA. It is easy for one who has never been a farmer to tell the farmer what to do. But Bill No. C-100 should give the farmer the means to set up his farm as he sees fit, the opportunity to operate and modernize his farm and to plan and improve his farm production.
The clauses of this bill should include ways of actually helping the farmer. But, no. We have, as I said on many occasions, economists like my excellent friend for Matapedia-Ma-tane (Mr. Tremblay), others like my very good friend the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), especially of the forests of Iles-de-la-Madeleine, able to suggest plans to farmers. We are satisfied and we rejoice when we see

the ARDA program being organized in eastern as well as in western Canada, but ARDA was more particularly established to help underdeveloped and depressed areas of our province.
We have had a great number of agricultural plans from economists, sociologists and others in Canada for the last 25 or 30 years. Suggestions and plans have not been lacking. But there has been a terrible and complete lack of suggestions liable to really help the farmer.
Of course, we have heard these people, like others, during election campaigns, bewailing the farmer's lot, stating energetically that farming was the basis, the foundation of the whole economy and of the social and economic structure of this country. However, in 1964 more than ever, we find that agriculture is slowing down, that the farmer is getting less recognition than ever, that the farming class is the most scoffed at and the least considered, the most ill-treated by the government at present.
Mr. Chairman, the farmer deserves more than what he is getting at the present time.
The other day, I referred to some facts concerning colonization and agriculture. In those days, with the assistance of the federal government, we implemented plans like those of Rogers, in Ottawa, and Auger, in Quebec, to promote the back-to-the-farm movement in the northern part of the province; we told people living in the cities of Montreal, Ri-mouski, Three Rivers, Quebec and elsewhere: Come and settle on farms, join the back-to-the-farm movement; it is the only way to fight effectively against the unemployment crisis in Canada. At that time, especially during the years 1934 and 1935, we promoted colonization in the province of Quebec and in some other provinces. Today, we visit those same settlements where 200 or 250 families had settled in 1934 and we find hardly 50, 60 or 75 families. Why? Because the farmer can no longer earn his living on the farm. In fact, he has to leave it, wander in the bush and work in mines or in factories, in order to earn enough money to allow him to carry on the operation of his farm, where he can no longer earn a livelihood for himself, his wife and children.
Mr. Chairman, is this Bill No. C-100 likely to help that farmer? Is it also likely to help to house or to settle farmers on those farms which have been vacant for ten years? No.
A bill is introduced which in its simplicity tells us all the good will of the Minister of Agriculture to help the farmer by allowing

him to borrow larger amounts than he used to do in the past, to help him in borrowing for his son or a member of his family who wants to settle on a farm.
But such is neither the problem, nor the solution.
Even if we would help with $10,000, $15,000 or $25,000 a farmer to settle his son or settle himself, if he had no assurance that he will be able to sell his production, in five, ten or 15 years from now, we will still be faced with a more acute problem, more serious than the one facing us now.
As I said, there are possibilities to help the farmer, but not with half measures, nor by introducing in the house a bill like Bill No. C-100, because in itself this means that it is absolutely necessary to increase the indebtness of the farmer.
I had the opportunity to visit farmers in western Canada. I went to Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia and also to Manitoba. I saw there farmers who though owning thousands of acres of land, nevertheless have been deeply in debt for the past 10 or 15 years, since the massive crop failures, or since some crops did not sell, or ever since the crops have been sold to China, or communist Russia.
The problem of the western farmers is far from being solved. The same is true for the problem of the eastern farmers which was never considered until 1964.
I very much doubt that the Minister of Agriculture is quite aware of what is happening in eastern Canada. I am rather inclined to believe that the minister who is actively responsible for ARDA knows more about the needs of the eastern farmers in this country than the present Minister of Agriculture. That is, to a certain extent, why my good friend, the minister responsible for ARDA was, earlier today, sitting beside the official Minister of Agriculture, to brief him on what is happening in eastern Canada, and more particularly in the province of Quebec.
The bill in which we are asked to award generous, or more important, loans to farmers, has our approval, except for one or two clauses where we cannot accept the interest rates suggested by the Minister of Agriculture.
It is not only in respect of the Department of Agriculture that we object to interest rates which will double any debt in 20 years and treble it in 25 years. We are opposed to all those interest rates suggested by any department or minister who would introduce such bills.
We are in favour of the spirit or the principle of this bill which is aimed at helping the farmer, but we are firmly opposed to the
Farm Credit Act
hidden spirit of the bill, which is to take unfair advantage of the farmer. We are going to stand up against it. In fact, we are going to move-I think the hon. member for Comp-ton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe) is going to do it -an amendment to do away with the rate of interest which will oblige a farmer to repay 20 years from now twice the amount borrowed in 1964.
This is all I have to say on the bill at this stage. When the agricultural question is more thoroughly discussed, I will come back to it, and I hope that the Minister of Agriculture will listen carefully to our suggestions. In certain circles, there is still a tendency to ridicule our suggestions and proposals, but the time will come soon when the minister, as well as the government, will have to face the financial problem which prevents agriculture to progress as it should, as the system which prevents all departments, the Canadian legislation and all Canadian economy from developing as it should be possible in our country.
Let us save agriculture first and then we will save the whole country.

I shall be very brief, Mr. Chairman. One thing just occurred to me after I sat down, and it is with regard to the $235 million which farmers receive at present from sources other than government sponsored lending services. I believe the minister sought to leave the impression that this legislation would take up most of that slack, if you want to call it that. That was a misleading impression to me because most of the people who have borrowed this money have gone to other sources as a last resort. In many cases they first approached the banks, the farm improvement loans authority, the Farm Credit Corporation, credit unions and so on, and when they exhausted these they went to other sources to get the money, sometimes at higher interest rates.
If I draw the right conclusion I take it the government will have legislation to introduce to increase the amounts available under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Such legislation, in my opinion, should have come before us prior to this bill. On reading clause 16 in particular I cannot help but wonder whether the government is contemplating an increase in the interest rates on farm improvement loans. Could he let us know whether this is so or not?

Mr. Chairman, when I indicated that farmers used $235 million worth of credit over and above government sponsored

Farm Credit Act
loans, I should have made it clear that we hope, with the three pieces of legislation we are going to bring before parliament, they will take care of most of it. subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: Can the minister assure the committee that the interest rate will be maintained at 5 per cent, thus continuing the same policy we had?

speechtext: I address my question to the minister because he knows very well that the income of farmers in eastern Canada is very low. I appeal to the minister and the government not to change the policy with respect to the 5 per cent loans.
