speechtext:
We feel quite strongly about this and we believe the farmer should be looked after, but when he gets a loan over $27,500, a supervised loan, we feel it should be made at an economic rate. When I speak of an economic rate I mean the amount which the government has to pay for money it borrows, plus the cost of operating the Farm Credit Corporation and a reasonable amount for bad debts, possibly not more than one quarter of 1 per cent, and probably not less than one eighth of 1 per cent. This would give us an opportunity to take more risks so far as loans to farmers are concerned.
Again I go back to the study which the Quebec department of agriculture made. With all respect to my hon. friend who has just spoken, I am a little familiar with farming in eastern Canada. At one time I owned six farms in eastern Canada and I had to make a living farming.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: How often have you visited the province of Quebec since you became minister?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
In all humbleness, I have been to many of the farms in Quebec, and discussed agricultural problems with the deputy minister of agriculture from Quebec. The Quebec study indicates that their whole salvation is dependant on larger economic units. They feel quite keenly about this. They feel that a farmer, if he is a milk producing farmer, must have at least a minimum 100,000 pounds contract a year, with a 100 acre farm, to make a go of it.
If he is going to produce beef cattle, if he is involved in a cow and calf proposition, then he has to have a minimum of 50 cows

and at least 300 acres. 1 might remind hon.
members that from 1941 to 1956 we lost an average of 1J per cent of our farmers per year to the urban centres, and in the period from 1956 to 1961 we lost 3J per cent of our farmers because of their moving to urban centres. This process is just not going to stop. The number of farmers moving off the land is going to increase. I do not think there is any doubt about that. So far as the interest is concerned, we feel that this is the proper approach and we would hope that hon. members would feel the same as we do.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: One last question. Suppose under the bill you fix the interest rate at 5 per cent with no restriction. What amount of money will the government lose if the interest rate is fixed at 5 per cent generally?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I address this question because I remember that the late C. D. Howe said in the house a few years ago, "What's a million'', in regard to the army and navy. However, so far as the farmers are concerned the income of farmers in eastern Canada is so low that I think it is the duty of the minister and the government to make sacrifices for the farmers. The average income of eastern farmers is about $1,200 a year. That is why I address this question. We spend $1J billion for defence, and I am surprised at the minister's interest in the farmers when the income of eastern farmers is so low. I prefer to fight for Canadians rather than to spend money for nothing sometimes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Before we proceed with the details of the bill I should like to comment on what the minister said with regard to the $235 million. He suggested the bill would help to alleviate outside borrowing of this $235 million. Surely he must realize that the greater part of the $235 million is short term credit. He himself has said, as found in Hansard, that the act is in no way designed to meet the short term credit requirements of farmers.
I am also concerned about his remarks a few minutes ago with regard to the $27,500 limit. He suggested that an interest rate of 5 per cent was a subsidized rate. He suggested, too, that anybody borrowing more money than $27,500 did not need the subsidized rate. Do I gather correctly from his remarks that anybody borrowing more than $27,500 was borrowing for an operation large enough that he did not need the subsidized rate and could well afford to pay what he termed the economic rate? If this is so, then I can only assume that the large amounts of money provided by these amendments are, in the opinion of the minister, a direct help for the large farmer. This is what I have suspected all along.
Certainly, the minister suggests that 5 per cent interest on $27,500 is a subsidized rate and that anybody borrowing more than that can well afford to pay the going rate. If I interpret him correctly, the going rate will be 5f per cent plus .87 per cent, plus { per cent for bad debt writeoff. This would make the total interest close to 6J per cent. If one takes the difference between 5 per cent on $40,000 or $50,000 and 6 J per cent on the same amount of money over a 30-year period, he will find that it amounts to close to $15,000 more the farmer is going to have to earn from saleable products to pay the interest. I should like to see a provision for the 5 per cent interest rate written into the bill.

The minister said that he gathered from my remarks that I was against raising the ceiling on loans to $40,000 and $55,000 under part III. I am not against it. However, I have a suspicion that in doing this we will narrow the field of the Farm Credit Corporation. I appreciate the fact that there are many young farmers who, in buying a well established farm, will need more than $20,000 or $27,500.
I suspect that these amendments will narrow rather than broaden the field of activities of the corporation. I gather from the minister's remarks that anybody borrowing less than $27,000 does not have an economic unit and therefore deserves the subsidized rate, whereas anyone borrowing more than $27,500 has an economic unit and can borrow at what he calls the economic rate. I suggest this is not a good rule of thumb to apply. There may well be many a young farmer who wishes to buy his father's farm or his neighbour's farm, and who may well need to borrow $40,000. However, such a farmer will need a stabilized rate of interest at 5 per cent.
I should like to think that the minister wholeheartedly believes that agriculture needs a stabilized rate of 5 per cent. I suggest this in all seriousness. Let us suppose that a young farmer under 45 years of age wishes to buy a farm. He is prepared to buy a farm that is a going concern, which will cost about $40,000. If these amendments are passed the farmer can borrow $40,000 from the Farm Credit Corporation. However, he could also borrow $27,000 at 5 per cent from the Farm Credit Corporation and borrow the other $13,000 to buy equipment from the bank through the Farm Improvement Loans Act, after the government has increased the amount available under that act. He can borrow this money at 5 per cent, too. He therefore saves himself money by breaking the deal into two parts and borrowing the total amount at 5 per cent interest rather than paying the 6| per cent on that additional $13,000.
If the minister follows my quick calculations, I am sure he will realize that in introducing this bill providing for two rates of interest he does not simplify farm borrowing; he complicates it. He does not do away with the red tape which the farmers hate so much; he adds to the red tape and the difficulties connected with acquiring a loan. I am very much afraid that he aids more large farmers than he does small ones.
There is another point I hope the government has considered, and that is the effect the availability of these large amounts of

money will have on the cost of land. We farmers realize that the price of land has risen tremendously in the last few years. The high cost of land is, perhaps, beneficial to those elderly farmers who are about to sell their property. However the high cost of land is a burden which the practising farmer must bear, and it brings him no real benefit. Certainly there is some fear in my mind as to the effect this $40,000 and $55,000 provision will have on the price of land. This fear was substantiated when the farmers union was in Ottawa about a month ago and suggested that the ceiling on loans from the Farm Credit Corporation remain as it is. They thought if there were an increase it would cause a tremendous increase in the price of land. I throw out this suggestion to the minister and I hope he and his officials will consider it, because the cost of land has risen tremendously in the last six or seven years. It is a burden around the necks of the farmers now operating land and certainly we, as legislators, do not want to add to this burden in any way.
While I believe that the amendments may be needed, I do not think the interest rates should fluctuate on the higher amounts. If the minister is determined to increase the ceiling on loans to $40,000 and $55,000, and I am not opposed to that although I do not believe the increase needs to be that high, then the interest rate should be spelled out in the bill. It should remain at the flat 5 per cent which is the rate charged for a farm improvement loan. If an increase is brought about, that will not necessarily reduce the loss the Farm Credit Corporation has suffered this year and the year previous.
I can remember that when I first came to Ottawa the old farm loan board was making money and, in fact, paid income tax I thought this was an error. While we have not seen much evidence of it yet, this government was supposed to be against high interest rates and was going to make every effort to reduce operating costs. Perhaps in the foreseeable future the government will be borrowing money at less than 5 per cent and will thus reduce the loss suffered by the Farm Credit Corporation. I can see that with the amount of money the Farm Credit Corporation is lending and the amount that is being repaid them every year, they will be able to lend money at 5 per cent in the near future and still break even. This is all we want to see them do. I hope that before we continue a clause by clause study of this bill the minister will make a decision with regard to the 5 per cent 20220-267J
Farm Credit Act
interest rate which will be applicable to these larger loans. I should like to see the government set the rate of interest by statute on all moneys borrowed from the Farm Credit Corporation.

speechtext: Before the minister answers, I wonder if he would clear up this point with regard to the interest rate which is to apply on that portion of the amount in excess of $27,500? speechtext: That is right. It is the same as the National Housing Act provisions. subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: Is he in the same position as a man who borrows money under the Small Loans Act which parliament has on the statute books?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: I should point out that our statistics indicate that farmers pay between 10 and 15 per cent on the $235 million which, as I mentioned earlier, are borrowed outside the Farm Credit Corporation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: On short term loans.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
As far as farmers are concerned, we have been able to borrow as low as 4i per cent. The amounts we are speaking of are subject to repayment over 20 years and the rate would be 5| per cent, as I indicated earlier.
When we were putting together the amendments to this act we were thinking about

Farm Credit Act
eastern farmers in particular, farmers in Quebec and adjacent areas. Take a unit in Quebec of 300 acres of land; we know that in most of these areas grass will support between 50 and 75 cows on a unit of this size. If farmers are engaged with a cow and calf proposition, add something like one and a half tons of hay throughout the winter. If they are trying to sell the calf as part of an operation where it is given to the feeder, gross earnings from this land would be about $7,500 a year. If a farmer were to borrow $40,000, his payment on the first $20,000 would be $1,322 a year and his payment on the other $20,000 would be $1,551, so his gross payment plus taxes would be $2,873. If he were a fairly good operator and he had a good average crop he should net somewhere between $4,000 and $4,500. This process would certainly lift him out of the economic position in which he finds himself today, a position which it is almost impossible to sustain. It is very similar to the project in the Abitibi area on which ARDA was doing a lot of work this year. In this instance the farmer had a minimum of 50 cows. We felt this would be a step in the right direction, together with other bills and amendments such as farm improvement loans, the machinery bill, and so on. This will not mean a cure overnight but it seems to me it is the proper approach.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
A millionaire's
approach.

speechtext:
Well, the hon. member can speak for himself. I know he does not need this sort of loan-he owns half of the Hanna district; I realize that. My feeling is for the farmer and I think we can do something for him on this basis.
In answer to the hon. member's question in connection with interest rates, we think it is reasonable to think that the man who can afford this $25,000 will receive a good deal less criticism if he can stand up and face the world and say: I am paying what I am supposed to pay and I can make a living doing this.

speechtext:
I was thinking that we do not make this kind of distinction in connection with the Small Businesses Loans Act. As I recollect it, loans are made there up to $50,000 and I am almost certain-I read the act some months ago-that there is no distinction between the rate of interest for any part of the loans. The loans are guaranteed by the government at a fixed rate of interest and it is not required that up to $27,500

one interest rate will be charged and that over this amount another rate will apply. It seems to me that when we are making loans to farmers the same interest rates should apply throughout. Why do we make this distinction with reference to farmers borrowing these larger sums? The ceiling for the farmer in part II of this bill is lower, as I recall it, than the ceiling in the Small Businesses Loans Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: I am busy trying to run the Department of Agriculture. They have not promoted me that far yet.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: To close the matter as far as I am concerned, let me say that the minister may be busy running the Department of Agriculture-that, of course, is his job- but the government surely has the responsibility to preserve some degree of equity in treating the different economic groups in Canada. It seems to me that in the new provisions which the minister is introducing he is inserting a principle which is different from that which applies to other economic groups and I hope when we get to the various clauses he will reconsider his stand on this matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister indicated that the increase was intended particularly to aid farmers in Quebec and to help them establish economic units. speechtext: In the year 1962-63 the average loan in Quebec was the highest in any province of Canada, with the exception of British Columbia. There is a great need, and these people appreciate how to use credit. I think this is the very thing they need to help them out of many of their difficulties. The government of Quebec has recognized this with regard to these loans of $20,000 by paying 2i per cent of the interest rate. I think this is something other provinces should consider in their programs to help farmers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: In what province were the highest losses? Did they correlate with the highest loans? Can any comparison be made?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.

speechtext: Do I gather from the Minister's remarks that he thinks farmers borrowing more than $27,500 can well afford to pay these high interest rates? This is the impression I had. Is it a correct impression?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes. I think it is a big step forward, when we know he was paying between 10 per cent and 18 per cent for this money.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: You do not know anything of the kind. You suggested that $235 million was borrowed outside the Farm Credit Corporation; but these were short term borrowings, not long term. I gather from the minister's remarks that he believes anybody borrowing $27,500 is a big farmer and can well afford to pay a higher rate of interest. This is my interpretation of the minister's remarks, and I would like to know if this is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext: As I suggested, we are not changing what has taken place before. The farmer can borrow $27,500 at 5 per cent; the act will not change. What we are doing is broadening it to help the farmer who is operating a good, economic unit. There is provision in the act whereby under certain circumstances you cannot even borrow money. I do not suppose the hon. member could obtain a loan; he is in such good shape that he would not be permitted to borrow money under this act. But this provision is for farmers who need help. I am saying, Mr. Chairman, that we are not changing this provision, but any additional amount shall be borrowed at an economic rate. I think this is justifiable and we stand behind it. I think the farmers will accept it and will think it is a great deal better than they had before.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister has perhaps led the house to believe that I am not in need of a loan. I would like to correct that false impression; I certainly am in need of a loan. I live in the dry part of Alberta where the grass is short and the water is scarce, and if the minister can do anything to help us in that area, I would greatly appreciate it. If he could give me a loan under the Farm Credit Corporation, my banker and I would both greatly appreciate it, but being a member of parliament I am excluded from obtaining a loan. However, I would like to think that many of those borrowing more than $27,500 would be small farmers, young farmers who need that much money and cannot afford to pay a high rate of interest on a high borrowing. This runs
Farm Credit Act
into a terrific amount of money. As I suggested, the difference between a $40,000 and $55,000 borrowing is $15,000 over 30 years, which comes to something like $500 more interest each year than a young farmer who is buying an economic unit would have to pay in interest alone to Harry Hays & Company, if I may use that term. I say that this high rate of interest on high borrowing is a millionaire's approach, and only a millionaire would think this would benefit the small farmer in any way, shape or form.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not be very long, but I want to say a few words on Bill No. C-100 to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski)-which, to my mind, seems most logical-to set up, if need be, an appeal board concerning loans of the Farm Credit Corporation.
A while ago, the minister said that he knew the Quebec region fairly well and he even informed us that, at one time, he had owned five farms in that region. That assertion puzzles me a little. I wonder whether he owned those farms to operate them or to trade them. There are so many of those people, especially in my riding. Indeed, I could name large land buyers who have never seen the colour of the land and evidently never farmed it, and who own up to 40 lots in my region. The fact that they own them is precisely detrimental to those lots, since they bought them for a few hundred dollars from their owners, and they claim three times what they paid. If that is how- I do not mean, far from it, that he proceeded in that way-but if that is how the minister, at one time, owned farms in the province of Quebec, I don't agree with him at all, because we have too many of those people who own farms and who are not farmers.
What we want-and let us hope this will be made easier by the amendments brought in to Bill No. C-100, is to establish average units, but not everywhere, obviously, because all Quebec farmers would not benefit from them. In fact, most of our farmers own family farms, and we cannot rely on those larger units the Quebec minister is now trying to lure us with, those units of at least 500 acres.
If you want our Quebec farmers to stop thinking of the land and of the family farm as it stands now, if you keep on trying to impose upon them a minimum of 500 acres

Farm Credit Act
for each farm, all you have to do is to introduce here the Russian plan and your success is guaranteed.
As for us, we are in favour of the family farm system and so are our farmers. For two years, I have been actively looking after farm loans in my riding, and I must say that we succeeded last year, by our efforts, in having 15 per cent of the applications accepted by the Farm Credit Corporation. I want the minister to note these figures and to consider that if only 15 per cent of the applications were accepted by the Farm Credit Corporation in the Lake St. John area, there is certainly something wrong.
1 heard the minister say that over 40 per cent of the loans were accepted. This is certainly not the case in the province of Quebec.
In my riding, hardly 15 per cent of applications have been accepted and still, the amounts have not all been paid, because only 10 per cent of loans approximately have actually been made.
After looking into the matter and having talked to farmers in an attempt to find the trouble, I reached the conclusion that credit advisers were to blame. I feel that the trouble lies with credit advisers. The minister said earlier that he was familiar with certain areas of the province of Quebec. I am convinced, however, that he does not know it through and through. The minister is not aware of the partisanship existing in the province of Quebec. This is not to our credit, but I must say this, because I found last year that half the applications for loans were being turned down because of political partisanship.

Their role is precisely to encourage farmers to stay on the farm. That is why we say that credit advisers must organize their work so as to put an end to farm abandonment. In fact, that makes ten families which have been chased away from their farm when they should have been provided with the necessary means to stay on the farm.
It is rightly said that the purpose of the amendments under consideration is to help our farmers. Well, then, let us help them properly. At present, they are given loans, about the same way a real estate agent would do it, and they are told: "You wish to get out of the hole? Then borrow now and borrow again tomorrow."
Moreover, it is said that agriculture is the basis of the economy. If we really want to help the farmer, since agriculture is the basis of the economy, let us help them by the granting of a monetary contribution.
Mr. Chairman, I have heard the minister state a while ago that he borrows money at 4 or 4J per cent. I ask him whether he ever

Farm Credit Act
helped farmers, whose production is the basis of our economy, through our monetary system, namely the Bank of Canada? There is the means. Let him stop borrowing money. The situation is such that in order to help the farmer, the government makes him borrow money and it borrows money itself so that it may lend the farmer more money.
Does the minister work for the finance companies or for the farmers?
We want him to work more for the benefit of the farmers and, to do so, he should make better use of the Bank of Canada. If only he would grant loans at the administrative costs he would then really help them. In fact, it is the only way to help them; he would thus grant them loans on the very basis of our economy.
But if he wishes to continue to use our silly financial system, he should at least lend at a rate of interest of 5 per cent, but he should exempt farmers from taxes. The government gives industry such an exemption. He should exempt farmers from taxes during a five or ten year period, to give them an opportunity to recover and then he would really come to the farmers rescue. As for the suggestion of the hon. member for Mackenzie who would like to establish an appeal board, I suggest that in the Lake St. John area, in Chicoutimi and Roberval, which he seems to know fairly well, the minister should appoint the county council, an organization entirely free from political affiliations, because members of the appeal board should not have anything to do with politics. The farmer who will apply for a loan must also obtain justice from this non-partisan group, not to mention that the county council is a regional organization which knows farmers well and will do them justice.
I feel that this suggestion of the hon. member is the best one made tonight. The appointment of such a group would finally help farmers whose applications for loans have been turned down for the reasons I mentioned earlier.
I would say to the minister: "Why not take the trouble to send into our area someone who would examine the situation on the spot. Stop relying on such and such an official. Go and examine the situation yourself and you will put your finger on what is wrong now." I could tell him that today, instead of helping the farmer, we are making things more difficult for him.

Surely a qualified lawyer in a particular area, regardless of his politics, should be able to act on behalf of the Farm Credit Corporation. We spent a great

The farmers have to pay them in the end, and I know what happens in my area and other areas as well. There are only five accredited lawyers in my whole constituency. It so happens that all of them are Liberals. It so happens that we appointed them farm credit solicitors. When the government changed, the new government changed all the solicitors and cut off these lawyers regardless of whether or not they were doing a good job. It was pure and simple patronage.
The minister has said on many occasions that he does not want any part of political patronage, and I agree with him. As a fellow Albertan he is on the right track. But let him talk to the political organizers, particularly in the cities of Edmonton and Calgary, who control the legal patronage lists. Let us talk in practical terms. Let him not supply answers like he did to me, saying the Barrhead is 25 miles from Edson and the farmers can go over there. I am sure he appreciates where the rivers run in Alberta. I am sure he also appreciates where the roads are. If he is going to continue to make these farmers drive 125 miles to see a lawyer in Edmonton who is no more competent than the lawyers we have in Edson and Barrhead, it is absolute nonsense and a farce.
The minister is increasing the limits under the act and this is fine and dandy. I agree with it; but in increasing the limits he is going to increase the fees paid to the lawyers. He and I also know that these contracts are drawn up by clerks in the offices of the lawyers. subtopic: SASKATCHEWAN
subsubtopic: REQUIREMENT THAT RECIPIENTS WORK FOR AID GIVEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, June 8, as recorded at page 4033 of Hansard, I put this question to the government:
Is the federal government aware of the declaration made by a minister of the Saskatchewan government that it intends to require recipients of social aid to work for relief? Have any proposals been made to the federal government regarding this matter, and what is the attitude of the federal government toward such a proposal?
It was felt by Mr. Speaker that the question was not one to be dealt with on orders of the day so I asked that it be transferred to be taken up in one of these overtime periods.
I hope we may now get an answer from one of the ministers or from one of the parliamentary secretaries.
It seems to some of us that this announcement from Saskatchewan is a very serious one, and that every effort should be made to prevent such a retrograde step being taken. It is our hope that the federal government will have no part in any such proposal. All of us believe in work rather than relief, but we do not believe in work for relief. This was well put on Monday of last week in an editorial in the Toronto daily Star, a sentence or two of which I should like to read. Speaking of this Saskatchewan proposal the Star said:
If it meant that a concerted effort should be made to find normal jobs for the unemployed and thus take them off the relief rolls, every reasonable person would be for it. What the advocates of this policy really want in most cases, however, is to make everyone on relief who can walk put in a few hours every day at some kind of physical labour, however pointless.
Later in the same editorial I note the following sentence or two:
A program of forced labour for people on relief can only serve as a means of punishment and humiliation for those involved, while disorganizing the province's regular public works system. It also has possibilities of course, for getting certain jobs done on the cheap, and undercutting the wages of civic and provincial workers.

(Subject matter of questions debated under adjournment motion).
I believe this editorial and others which I have seen in various newspapers make it very clear that any step of this nature would be thoroughly retrograde in character. It reminds us of policies which were practised

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion by a number oi governments in the 'thirties. We have got over those policies; let us not go back to them. A policy of this kind is against everything that people who are practised in the field of social welfare stand for; they have already made it clear that they hope such a policy will not be pursued. I should like to remind the house, also, of the statement made the other day by the Canadian Labour Congress in which, among other things, it was pointed out that this practice would be contrary to the universal declaration of human rights which declares that everyone has a right to work, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment, but also that everyone has a right to free choice of employment.
So, because we feel this is a backward step which should not be entertained, and because it would seem to us that if any change in the Unemployment Assistance Act is to be made, the federal government is involved, we hope the federal government through its spokesman tonight will make it clear that it will have no part in a retrograde policy of this kind.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):

speechtext:
I am not too sure that this is the proper place in which to conduct a campaign against the government of Saskatchewan which, in effect, is what the hon. member is doing. As far as I am aware, all that has happened is that some statements have been reported in the press, some of which have not been very complete. Certainly, the federal government has received no firm statement or declaration from the government of Saskatchewan even one asking for consideration of a change in the type of the present program. So I think the point made by the hon. member is academic at the moment.
I do not know what the hon. minister- Mr. Boldt, I believe it was-said. Perhaps the hon. member knows no more than we do, except that from various press reports he read or heard over television or radio. I do not know if he has a word for word statement of what the minister said; the government has not, to my knowledge.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The minister said he wrote to the federal government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Well, we have not received anything; we have received no communication setting out any type of proposal which he would even like us to consider. The last

discussion there was on these lines was of a most general nature. It took place at the last welfare conference with federal and provincial ministers a week and a half or two weeks ago.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: What was the position of the government at that time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It was just a general discussion at that time on the Unemployment Assistance Act and what changes may be necessary, without really any detailed reference to this question of work for relief. Various provinces were asked to submit their views on it. They indicated they had certain views, and in a spirit of federal-provincial co-operation, I suppose, their points of view on this question have to be considered. At the time of the conference no specific proposals were advanced. I think the stand any federal government would have to take, in view of the fact that this is a shared field, would be that their proposals would have to be considered, once we have any proposals. We have not even received a proposal from the province of Saskatchewan; therefore I do not think there is any justification for the hon. member's alarm, certainly at this point.
What position did the federal government take when this matter was discussed at the conference?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It really was not discussed. It was indicated by certain provinces, I believe and I could not even tell you which ones now; perhaps it was one at that time, and it was not Saskatchewan-that they had some views on this subject. That aspect of the matter having been opened up, the provinces were asked to submit their proposals and have them ready for the next meeting. Since one province had views on this question it was felt it should be discussed. And that is about where the matter stands.

maintopic: AIRPORTS-MALTON-LIMOUSINE AND TAXI SERVICE BY UNLICENSED COMPANY
AIRPORTS-MALTON-LIMOUSINE AND TAXI SERVICE BY UNLICENSED COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon during the question period I asked the Minister of Transport whether he could advise this house why the Department of Transport in 1961 granted an exclusive privilege to Air Terminal Transport Limited to operate a limousine and taxi service at Malton airport when the company does not hold a taxi licence from either metropolitan Toronto or the township of Toronto in Peel county.
This question has been prompted by a situation which has arisen in Toronto where the Toronto taxicab conference is demanding
11. 1964	4227
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that they be given fair treatment in this Canada of ours, and that a monopoly that was granted by the previous government should be broken. I was amused a moment or two ago to hear the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm yell across the aisle his opposition to monopolies, and I heard two speakers on farm credit from Alberta claiming that they were also opposed to monopolies. Yet here we have a monopolistic agreement between the minister of transport for 1960 and 1961 and Air Terminal Transport Limited of 30 Howard Park avenue, Toronto which gives them, if I may quote from the front page of the indenture, which I was not able to secure from the previous government when I sat in opposition but which I got with ease from the present President of the Privy Council, (Mr. Mcllraith) in his earlier capacity of minister of transport, in December last year-
-the exclusive right and privilege (hereinafter referred to as the said right and privilege) to maintain and operate a limousine and taxicab station at the Malton international airport, at Malton in the province of Ontario, for the operation of a limousine and taxi service.
In this agreement between the then minister of transport and Air Terminal Transport Limited, which runs for ten years from 1960 to 1970, the word "taxi" is used ten times. The word "taxi" appears ten times in seven pages. This organization does not hold a taxi licence, either from the township of Toronto, in which Malton airport is situated, or from the municipality of metropolitan Toronto from which 98 per cent of their business originates.
There are 1,100 taxicab operators in the city of Toronto, all of whom are experienced and all of whom are seeking to give the taxicab service which this indenture is supposed to cover. I ask the Minister of Transport whether he will not look into this situation, which appears to be nothing but a dog in the manger attitude based on an exclusive franchise granted by the previous government.
This company do not supply a taxi service, yet they are given a contract which says that they alone shall supply a taxi service. I state that the 1,100 taxicab operators in Toronto who take fares out to Malton airport but are forbidden by the terms of this contract, it would appear, to pick up fares at Malton and bring them back into Toronto should be allowed to give the taxicab service people expect.
Why in the name of heaven should a monopoly be granted to a firm in Toronto to
4228	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion give taxicab or limousine service from the Malton airport? We do not do that here at the parliament buildings. If an hon. member wants a livery or taxicab at the front door of the buildings, this is government property and one of the officers at the door will call a number and summon one from downtown Ottawa. Or you can give him the number and he will call it. But at Malton airport and I am told the same situation prevails at Dorval and at Uplands, there is an exclusive agreement with one monopoly outfit to provide the service. Under the terms of the contract, whereby they pay 3f per cent of their gross revenue to the Department of Transport during the present five year period, X calculate that their gross take is $1,800,000 a year, and they do not have any competition, with the protection of the Department of Transport as per the agreement signed by the former minister of transport in 1961.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a nefarious attitude to take. I have gone to the trouble of looking up the taxicab bylaw of the township of Toronto, in which township the Air Terminal Transport Company have their offices. Under the old taxicab bylaw dated March 8, 1948 it is distinctly pointed out that,
-no person shall keep any motor vehicles whatever to be used for hire in the conveyance of persons from place to place within the township of Toronto or from any point within the said township to any point beyond the limits of the said township unless duly licensed therefor under the provisions of this bylaw.
The township of Toronto is a semi-rural district between Toronto and Hamilton. On December 31, 1956, a new bylaw was brought into effect covering taxicabs, and one clause which was added is very interesting.
"cab" means any vehicle used for hire for the conveyance of passengers either wholly within the municipality or to any point not more than three miles beyond its limits and includes a taxicab, ambulance, funeral hearse and sightseeing coach-
And note this:
-but does not include a limousine unless the limousine is equipped with a taxi meter;
Yet if you walk into the parliamentary library, there you have Webster's International dictionary, which is the first book you see in the library, and you will find it says a taxicab is a chauffeur driven automobile "'with or without a taxi meter." The general acceptance is a cab for hire with or without a taxi meter, but in the township of Toronto some fine hand, with a fine pallette, has painted a pretty picture, and has produced this clause which does not include a limousine unless it is equipped with a taxi meter. Therefore this

agreement that it shall provide a taxi service does not apply to a company which operates only limousines.
There are 16 hon. members from the Toronto area in this house, and since I was contacted this morning by the Toronto taxicab drivers conference I have spoken to six of them, and all of them advised me they are opposed to a monopoly operation in the city of Toronto at Malton airport.
There has been absolutely no tender on this $1,800,000 a year contract. Mr. Speaker, I have here a letter from the Department of Transport which contains the following paragraph:
When the agreement with Air Terminal Transport Limited was up for renewal in 1960, a tender call was considered but it was not possible to proceed on this basis because of the position taken by the provincial department of transport in respect to franchises.
I telephoned the Ontario provincial department of transport this morning and asked if there would be any trouble in securing a franchise to operate motor vehicles from Malton airport to Toronto if the federal government should issue a franchise, and I was advised there would be no trouble at all.

maintopic: AIRPORTS-MALTON-LIMOUSINE AND TAXI SERVICE BY UNLICENSED COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not had very much opportunity since the hon. member asked his question this afternoon to do any lengthy research into the matter. It is quite correct, as the hon. gentleman has said, that this particular company does have a contract which was renegotiated some years ago, I think in 1960. It is also true-at least I assume it is true because I read it in the Ottawa Journal this evening, that-
-eight taxi drivers seeking a test case they hope will permit them to pick up fares at Toronto international airport got what they wanted Wednesday-two summonses and eight $5 parking tickets.
I assume, therefore, this case is going to come into the courts and it would be perhaps unwise for me, under the circumstances, to attempt to say anything at this stage which might in any way prejudge a case that is going to be heard in the courts. But I listened with a great deal of interest to what the hon. member has said, and I will naturally continue my research into the subject and see whether there is in fact a situation which should be remedied and, if so, what the appropriate remedy should be.

Of course hon. members will realize that people travel by air presumably to get to their destinations quickly, and that there would be a great deal of dissatisfaction on the part of the travelling public if they arrived at an airport on a day which was stormy, when perhaps it would be more profitable for taxis to carry passengers in the metropolitan areas instead of going out to the airports to wait
11, 1964	4229
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion for passengers. In this case there might be nobody there to carry them. It is important to have some means of assuring the public that there will be a means of getting to and from airports at all times, but whether the present system is the best one I am not prepared to say.
